items.title: Small business survival rates are lower than commonly thought
items.claim: ONS UK Business Demography statistics consistently show what 5-year survival rate for new UK businesses?

options.text: Around 40% — roughly six in ten new UK businesses don't survive five years

items.reveal_title: Most new businesses don't make it
items.reveal:
ONS Business Demography data: of UK enterprises born in 2017, 39.6% survived to 2022. Year-1 survival is around 90%; the attrition is concentrated in years 2-5. SME failure causes (UK Federation of Small Businesses surveys) cluster around cash flow, late payment, and lack of management capacity.

Entrepreneurship narratives in business teaching focus on success stories. The base rate is more sobering and is one reason support programmes (start-up loans, mentoring) emphasise survival skills over growth.
items.why: Survivor bias in business case studies hides the failure rate. A textbook with only successful firms gives a misleading picture of what running a business actually involves.

items.title: Ford's $5 day was a retention crisis fix, not generosity
items.claim: In January 1914, Henry Ford doubled the basic wage at his Highland Park plant to $5 a day. What problem was he solving?

options.text: Falling demand for the Model T
Catastrophic worker turnover — the assembly line was so monotonous that annual turnover had reached around 370%, meaning the plant had to hire roughly 50,000 people to maintain a workforce of 14,000
A unionisation drive he wanted to prevent

items.reveal:
Daniel Raff and Lawrence Summers's 1987 paper analysed Ford's wage decision. Turnover collapsed after the announcement; absenteeism dropped from 10% to 2.5%; productivity rose. The wage was conditional — there was a 'Sociological Department' that inspected workers' homes for 'good moral character' to qualify.

The popular story (Ford paid workers enough to buy his cars) is a post-hoc rationalisation. A Model T cost roughly $440; a workforce of 14,000 buying cars wouldn't move the market.

The wage was efficient: Ford gained productivity worth more than the extra wage bill.
items.why: Famous 'visionary' business decisions usually have boring, specific operational drivers. The $5 day looks like generosity; it was wage-efficiency arbitrage.

items.title: Maslow's pyramid was never drawn by Maslow
items.claim: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs is taught with a pyramid. What did Maslow himself draw?

options.text: He drew the pyramid himself in his 1943 paper
He never drew it as a pyramid; the pyramid representation was introduced by management consultants and textbooks in the 1960s
He drew it as a circle to indicate non-linear progression
He explicitly rejected any visual representation

items.reveal:
Todd Bridgman, Stephen Cummings and John Ballard's 2019 paper in the Academy of Management Learning & Education traced the pyramid to Charles McDermid's 1960 management article in Business Horizons. Maslow's 1943 'A Theory of Human Motivation' described needs as overlapping and dynamic — not rigidly tiered.

Maslow himself, late in his career, qualified the theory heavily: needs can be pursued in parallel, prioritisation varies by culture and individual, and self-actualisation isn't a 'top' level so much as a developmental orientation.

Empirical tests find weak support for the strict hierarchy.
items.why: The most-taught motivation diagram in business education was drawn by someone other than the named theorist and oversimplifies what he wrote. Worth checking what's in the textbook against what's in the source.
